findings.description: The MSCA-PF evaluation form (ef_he-msca_en.pdf, v2.2) explicitly lists 'consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project' as a sub-criterion under Excellence for MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships. The excellence section contains no explicit determination of whether the gender dimension is relevant to this research design (probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water diagnostics and irrigation decision support) and, if not relevant, no justification for its exclusion. The excellence-section claim_statuses contain no CL-entry addressing gender dimension in research design. Section 3.2 of the implementation section references ELTE's gender equality plan only as a legal compliance obligation, not as a reflection on research design. An evaluator cannot confirm this mandatory sub-criterion has been considered.
findings.evidence: No claim in the excellence validation_status addresses gender dimension in research methodology. Implementation section 3.2: 'Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is subject to the Horizon Europe requirement to hold and maintain a gender equality plan at grant signature and during the grant period' — framed as a compliance obligation only, not as engagement with gender dimension in research design.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit sub-paragraph to section 1.2 of the Excellence section either (a) identifying how the gender dimension is incorporated into the research design (e.g., diversity considerations in farmer engagement via AgroVIR, representativeness of field-validation sites, or disaggregated data collection in WP3), or (b) explicitly stating that the gender dimension is not applicable to this particular technical research design and providing a justification — as required by the evaluation criterion. Either treatment satisfies the sub-criterion; its complete absence does not.

findings.description: The evaluation form requires assessment of 'quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills'. The excellence section establishes Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's credentials through the PhD thesis reference (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527, summa cum laude 2020) and approximately four years of post-doctoral experience, but presents no list or summary of peer-reviewed publications, no count of international conference papers, no evidence of independent research output (open datasets, software releases), and no indication of peer recognition (journal reviewing, committee membership, fellowship or grant awards). For a competitive MSCA-PF evaluation where research independence is a key differentiator at postdoctoral career stage, the absence of an output record is a material gap in the researcher-profile sub-criterion.
findings.evidence: Excellence claim FELLOW: 'PhD summa cum laude 2020 on non-destructive evaluation of physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527); approx. 4 years post-PhD; expertise in non-destructive techniques for abiotic/biotic plant stress evaluation, crop monitoring, photosynthesis under stress, biostimulants.' No publication list, publication count, or evidence of independent research output appears in any section.
findings.recommendation: Add a concise publication and research-output summary to section 1.4 of the Excellence section listing key peer-reviewed publications by Dr. Cholakova (journal name, year, brief contribution statement), any conference presentations, open datasets, or open software contributions, and any evidence of peer recognition (reviewing activity, prizes, competitive grants). A structured CV in Part B-2 is separately required by the MSCA-PF application form, but the Part B-1 section 1.4 narrative must also make the researcher's track record legible to the evaluator.

findings.description: WP1 Task T1-03 explicitly states 'A Bayesian hierarchical model (or Gaussian process — model family decided at MS2 review)' for the core latent-field-state estimation model. While the Route A/Route B contingency architecture is a strength, presenting the primary model family itself as an open in-project choice may be read by evaluators assessing 'soundness of the proposed methodology' as insufficient methodological specificity at proposal stage. The evaluation criterion expects the principal modelling approach to be identified and justified, with alternatives documented as contingencies rather than co-primary unresolved options.
findings.evidence: Implementation section 3.1, T1-03: 'A Bayesian hierarchical model (or Gaussian process — model family decided at MS2 review) is fitted to the harmonised multi-sensor data to estimate root-zone soil moisture and crop water status as a posterior distribution with honest, calibrated uncertainty.'
findings.recommendation: In section 1.2 of the Excellence section, specify the primary model family for T1-03 (e.g., Bayesian hierarchical model, motivated by the multi-level structure of field, crop, and sensor sources) and frame the Gaussian process as an explicitly documented alternative if the hierarchical model proves computationally intractable, with a brief methodological justification for the primary choice. This preserves the scientific flexibility while satisfying the soundness-of-methodology sub-criterion.

findings.description: OBJ-5 and the excellence section's training and supervision sub-section explicitly and deliberately decline to pre-specify any quantitative targets for publications, training hours, thesis co-supervision, or career milestones, deferring all numerical commitments to the Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3). While the stated rationale is coherent (targets must emerge from the actual supervision relationship), MSCA-PF evaluators typically expect at least indicative minimum commitments at proposal stage. The complete absence of even indicative figures weakens the 'quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge' sub-criterion relative to competing proposals that specify minimum publication or training commitments.
findings.evidence: Excellence claim CL-16: 'OBJ-5 title: Advancement of the fellow's competences and career; measurable by D4-01 (Career Development Plan), training across MSCA-PF mandatory dimensions, peer-reviewed publication, two-way transfer evidenced by methods exchange; specific quantitative targets deliberately not pre-asserted.' Impact section 2.1 confirms the same deferral policy.
findings.recommendation: Add indicative minimum quantitative targets to section 1.3 of the Excellence section: for example, at least two peer-reviewed submissions during the fellowship; at minimum N hours of structured training per MSCA mandatory dimension; at least one documented knowledge-exchange event per project year. Make clear these will be confirmed and finalised in D4-01 with the supervisor, but provide enough specificity to allow evaluator assessment of the training programme's credibility.

findings.description: Section 2.2 describes the dissemination plan with conference presentations characterised only as 'at least one presentation per project year', with no named conference series, journal targets, or preprint repositories. The evaluation form sub-criterion 'suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan' requires quality assessment of the specific measures, not just the existence of a plan. Without named venues, an evaluator cannot assess whether the planned channels are well-matched to the project's target scientific communities in geoinformatics, remote sensing, and precision agriculture.
findings.evidence: Section 2.2: 'Conference activities are planned to occur at the rate of at least one presentation per project year and are recorded in D5-02 (Dissemination and communication activity report, due month 24).' No conference names, journal titles, or preprint platforms are mentioned in the dissemination plan.
findings.recommendation: Name at least two to three specific conference series relevant to the project's outputs (e.g., IEEE IGARSS, ISPRS Congress, ECPA European Conference on Precision Agriculture) and two to three target journal families (e.g., Remote Sensing of Environment, Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture) as indicative venues for OUT-1, OUT-2, and OUT-3 outputs. Specificity demonstrates familiarity with the dissemination landscape and makes the quality of the measures assessable.

findings.description: Section 2.3 correctly and explicitly declines to assert specific water-saving percentages, yield improvements, or economic return estimates (none appear in Tier 1-4 sources). However, the evaluation form sub-criterion 'magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts' requires evaluators to assess scale as well as mechanism. As drafted, the IMP-2 magnitude claim (water-use efficiency and farm resilience) is supported only by qualitative framing without any published background reference data contextualising the scale of the irrigation efficiency challenge in the target region or sector.
findings.evidence: Section 2.3: 'No specific water-saving percentages, yield improvement figures, or economic return estimates are asserted in any Tier 1–4 source for this project, and no such figures are invented here. The magnitude of IMP-2 at the project scale is properly described as: the first validated end-to-end demonstration that an uncertainty-aware multi-sensor fusion-to-WUE-irrigation-decision pipeline is technically feasible on real field data for tomato horticulture.'
findings.recommendation: Add two to three published background statistics on the scale of the irrigation efficiency challenge in the target region or sector (e.g., EUROSTAT irrigated area data for Hungarian horticulture, FAO water-use benchmarks for tomato, agronomic literature on yield losses from late stress detection) to contextualise why a successful TRL 3-4 demonstration matters at scale. No project-level economic projections should be added; the background data grounds the magnitude claim without overstating what TRL 3-4 delivers.

findings.description: The fellowship includes no formal non-academic placement or secondment; inter-sectoral exposure is provided entirely through AgroVIR's associated-partner role (field access and farmer feedback). Section 2.1's career-development narrative treats Dr. Jung's co-founder experience (Cubert GmbH, Brightic Research) as the primary inter-sectoral supervisory credential. While credible, the absence of any formal time embedded in a non-academic organisation limits the concreteness of the inter-sectoral career-development claim for the 'credibility of the measures to enhance career perspectives and employability' sub-criterion, particularly for evaluators who assess inter-sectoral exposure as a direct MSCA-PF outcome.
findings.evidence: Implementation section 3.2: 'There are no secondments in this fellowship. The full 24-month research programme is conducted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest.' Impact section 2.1 grounds inter-sectoral training in AgroVIR feedback and the supervisor's entrepreneurial background without describing any formal structured non-academic activity.
findings.recommendation: In section 2.1 of the Impact section, either (a) describe any structured activities with AgroVIR that go beyond field access — for example, documented user-requirements workshops, co-design sessions, or a technology-transfer demonstration with a formal time commitment — and frame these explicitly as inter-sectoral training activities; or (b) directly acknowledge the absence of a formal secondment and provide a stronger, evidence-based argument for why AgroVIR's operational feedback loop and Dr. Jung's entrepreneurial mentoring together constitute adequate inter-sectoral career development for the MSCA-PF objectives.

findings.description: Task T3-02 (non-destructive ground-truth collection) closes at month 20; Task T3-03 (uncertainty calibration and patch-covariation assessment) runs months 20-22 — a two-month window to conduct (a) prediction-interval coverage evaluation against the RQ5 criterion and (b) the Route B patch-covariation statistical test (RQ9). Both are demanding statistical analyses on seasonally collected field data. MS5 (month 22) requires both complete. The risk register (RISK-04 through RISK-06) addresses sparse ground truth and miscalibration risks but does not explicitly address the risk of insufficient analysis time between data collection close and MS5.
findings.evidence: Implementation section 3.1 Gantt: T3-02 active months 10-20; T3-03 active months 20-22. Section 3.1 MS5: 'Field validation and uncertainty calibration complete — Ground truth collected (RQ4); uncertainty-calibration metrics evaluated — prediction-interval coverage assessed against nominal (RQ5); Route B patch-covariation tested (RQ9).' No buffer between T3-02 close and T3-03 start is documented.
findings.recommendation: In section 3.1.6 or in the T3-03 task description, add explicit mitigation for the tight T3-03 window: for example, document that preparatory statistical scripting and protocol setup for the RQ5 and RQ9 analyses will be completed within T3-02 (months 18-20) so that quantitative analysis begins before data collection formally closes, or identify a contingency plan (e.g., partial-season data analysis protocol) if data collection is not fully complete by month 20.

findings.description: Section 3.2.2 states that ELTE 'is subject to the Horizon Europe requirement to hold and maintain a gender equality plan at grant signature and during the grant period' but does not confirm whether ELTE actually holds an active gender equality plan, nor whether ELTE holds the European Charter for Researchers HRS4R label. The evaluation form explicitly notes that 'institutions with the HRS4R label are exempted from providing further justification' for the hosting arrangements sub-criterion. Without a positive confirmation of either, an evaluator cannot determine whether ELTE meets the baseline institutional requirements for hosting quality.
findings.evidence: Section 3.2.2: 'Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is subject to the Horizon Europe requirement to hold and maintain a gender equality plan at grant signature and during the grant period, providing the institutional framework for gender equality obligations that apply throughout the fellowship.' No confirmation of an active GEP or HRS4R label is provided.
findings.recommendation: In section 3.2.2, add a factual statement confirming whether ELTE holds an active, published gender equality plan (including a reference URL if available) and whether ELTE holds the HRS4R label. If ELTE holds the HRS4R label, citing it explicitly satisfies the implementation criterion's hosting sub-element without further justification, per the evaluation form.

findings.description: Section 3.2 describes ELTE's hosting capacity almost exclusively through the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group and the supervisor's personal credentials. No information is provided about ELTE's broader institutional research profile, Horizon Europe or FP9 grant track record, ERA network memberships, international partnerships, or bibliometric standing in geoinformatics or agri-environmental modelling. Evaluators assessing 'quality and capacity of the host institutions and participating organisations' expect institutional-level evidence of research capacity, not only supervisor-level evidence.
findings.evidence: Section 3.2.2 focuses on: (1) the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group, (2) ELTE's administrative compliance functions, and (3) the supervisor's dual habilitations. No ELTE-level research profile indicators (grant history, ERA memberships, international collaboration record) are cited.
findings.recommendation: Add a short paragraph to section 3.2.2 summarising ELTE's institutional research profile relevant to the fellowship: any Horizon Europe or FP9 grants in geoinformatics or agri-EO contexts, ERA partnership network memberships, relevant bibliometric output in the field, and ELTE's institutional open-access and data-management policy framework. This grounds the host-capacity claim in verifiable institutional standing rather than relying solely on the supervisor's individual credentials.

revision_actions.action_description: Add an explicit gender-dimension paragraph to section 1.2 of the Excellence section. Either (a) identify how the gender dimension is incorporated into the research design — for example, diversity considerations in the farmer-engagement sample via AgroVIR, or representativeness considerations in ground-truth site selection in WP3 — or (b) explicitly state that the gender dimension is not applicable to this particular technical research domain and provide a one-paragraph justification. Either treatment satisfies the mandatory Excellence sub-criterion; its complete absence does not and will be flagged by evaluators.

Add a concise publication and research-output summary to section 1.4 of the Excellence section, listing key peer-reviewed publications by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova (journal name, year, brief contribution statement), any conference papers, open datasets, or open software contributions, and any evidence of peer recognition such as journal reviewing, competitive grants, or invited presentations. This evidence is essential for evaluators assessing the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills sub-criterion; its absence is a material gap for a competitive MSCA-PF application.

In section 1.2 of the Excellence section, specify the primary model family for WP1 Task T1-03 as the Bayesian hierarchical model, with a brief methodological justification (e.g., hierarchical structure matches the multi-level field/crop/sensor data architecture), and frame the Gaussian process as an explicitly documented fallback alternative if the hierarchical model proves computationally intractable at project scale. Remove the 'model family decided at MS2 review' framing that presents the core modelling choice as unresolved at proposal stage.

Add indicative minimum quantitative targets to section 1.3 of the Excellence section for the training programme: for example, at least two peer-reviewed journal submissions during the fellowship; a minimum of N structured training hours per MSCA mandatory dimension; at least one conference presentation per project year; at least one documented knowledge-exchange event per year at ELTE. State explicitly that these indicative floors will be confirmed and refined in D4-01 with the supervisor, preserving the principled deferral while giving evaluators a credibility anchor for the training sub-criterion.

In section 2.2 of the Impact section, name specific target venues for scientific dissemination: at minimum two to three relevant conference series (e.g., IEEE IGARSS, ISPRS Congress, ECPA European Conference on Precision Agriculture) and two to three target journal families (e.g., Remote Sensing of Environment, Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture) aligned with the project's OUT-1, OUT-2, and OUT-3 outputs. Also identify the preprint repository to be used for Plan S compliance. This specificity allows evaluators to assess the suitability of the dissemination measures against the target scientific communities.

In section 2.3 of the Impact section, add two to three published background statistics contextualising the scale of the irrigation efficiency challenge in the target region or sector — for example, EUROSTAT irrigated area data for Hungarian horticulture, FAO water-use benchmarks for tomato, or agronomic literature estimates of yield losses attributable to late stress detection. These data ground the IMP-2 magnitude claim without asserting project-level economic outcomes that a TRL 3-4 research fellowship cannot warrant. Cite sources explicitly so evaluators can verify the contextual scale claims.

In section 2.1 of the Impact section, either describe any structured technology-transfer or co-design activities with AgroVIR that go beyond field access (e.g., documented user-requirements workshops or feedback-loop sessions with a formal time commitment) and explicitly frame them as inter-sectoral training activities; or directly acknowledge the absence of a formal secondment and make a stronger evidence-based argument for why AgroVIR's operational feedback loop and Dr. Jung's co-founder mentoring together constitute credible inter-sectoral career development for the stated MSCA-PF employability objectives.

In section 3.1.4 (T3-03 task description) or section 3.1.6 (risk assessment), add explicit mitigation for the two-month T3-03 window: document that preparatory statistical scripting and analysis-protocol setup for the RQ5 and RQ9 assessments will be completed within T3-02 (months 18-20) so that quantitative analysis can begin before data collection formally closes at month 20, or specify a contingency analysis plan for partial-season data if full seasonal collection is delayed by weather or access constraints.

In section 3.2.2 of the Implementation section, add a factual statement confirming whether Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) holds an active, published gender equality plan (with a reference URL if publicly available) and whether ELTE holds the European Charter for Researchers HRS4R label. If ELTE holds the HRS4R label, cite it explicitly: this citation satisfies the hosting arrangements sub-criterion in the evaluation form without further justification per the form's explicit text.

In section 3.2.2 of the Implementation section, add a short paragraph summarising ELTE's broader institutional research profile relevant to the fellowship: Horizon Europe or FP9 grant history in geoinformatics or agri-EO contexts, ERA network or consortium memberships, relevant international research partnerships, and ELTE's institutional open-access and FAIR data policy. This provides evaluators with institution-level evidence for the 'quality and capacity of the host institution' sub-criterion that is independent of the individual supervisor's credentials.
